title: Opt-in tournament stack in the packaged deployment
description: Add the tournament stack to the released deployment as a compose profile that is off by default: Postgres, Redis, the tournament server, the identity service, one-shot services that fill the TMX and public-pages volumes and create the service account, and the Caddy routes. Turning it on is one documented step (enable the profile, then switch on 'Tournaments' in settings). Every secret is generated on the club's server on first start: the ES256 key pair and key id, the signer token, the service account password, the database password and the tournament server's unused JWT secret. Nothing is defaulted. Only Caddy is reachable from outside.

recommended_model.name: Opus 5.5
recommended_model.rationale: Multi-service deployment design with secret generation and health ordering.

acceptance_criteria: With the profile off, only the app and Caddy run, Caddy starts without the tournament services, and the app shows no tournament links
With the profile on, /tournaments and /public work under the club's own domain over HTTPS
Every secret is generated locally by one documented step; the compose file contains none, and startup fails clearly if one is missing rather than falling back to a default
The tournament server runs with JWT_ACCEPT_HS256=false and holds only the public key; the identity service holds the private key and has no JWT_SECRET
The app receives the service account password and the internal addresses of the tournament server and identity service only when the profile is on
The proxy routes and refusals are exactly those in the design note, section 4, including removal of the Cookie header on CourtHive routes
Services start in dependency order with health checks; memory limits: tournament server 512 MB, identity service 256 MB, Postgres 384 MB, Redis 64 MB
Disabling the profile later leaves tournament data intact on its volume
The paths /api/rankings and /epixodic at the origin root are answered with 404 by the proxy, not passed to the app

files_to_create: deploy/init-secrets.sh or an equivalent first-start step in the app CLI
notes: See docs/courthive_bundle_design.md (rewritten 2026-11-22 for latest upstream), sections 3 and 4. The test stack used there (compose file and Caddyfile) is the starting point.
The service account is created with: node src/scripts/admin-user.mjs ensure -e service@jim-dot-tennis.invalid -p <password> (inside the server image; exits 0 when it already exists).

Set on the tournament server: PERSONS_DISABLED=true, PERSONS_BASE_URL=disabled, DECLARATIONS_DISABLED=true, AMS_DISABLED=true, APP_MODE=production (the value 'development' enables a built-in administrator with a published password), TMX_URL=/tournaments/.
PEM keys work in an environment file as one line with \n escapes.

testing_requirements: Bring the stack up from nothing on a clean machine with the profile on and off

context.user_story: As a club operator, I want to switch tournaments on with one step.
context.programme: Club-readiness programme (sprints 019-024). Agreed constraints: BHPLTA clubs only; each club self-hosts its own instance; the original author must have no access to any other club's instance (no seeded accounts, no shared or default secrets, no phone-home); passkeys are the default sign-in with passwords as an optional fallback; the captain role is real; SQLite is the only supported database; CourtHive is bundled as an opt-in part of the package so clubs can run their own club championships.

status_note: Tested from nothing with the profile off and on, on-off-on with data kept, a missing secret, the proxy refusals, memory limits, and the app's client integration test inside the stack. Turning the profile off needs `docker compose --profile tournaments down` then `up -d`. The CourtHive images named in the compose file are not published yet.
